extracted.intended_audience: copywriters, marketers, and writers who want to make their copy funnier (especially for marketing/online content)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for using the Rule of 3 (triples) to make marketing and web copy funnier, including psychological rationale and concrete tactics for placement, cadence, punchline positioning, heightening, and where to apply the pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-part structure (beginning, middle, end)
rubrics_metrics.description: We like things with a beginning, middle, and end — stories, jokes, and even short copy feel satisfying when they resolve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure any anecdote or set-up has a clear ending; avoid stopping mid-story and expecting a laugh. Example anti-pattern: telling a story that never delivers an endpoint (the open-mic anecdote). Use the three-part structure to provide narrative closure before delivering humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum of three to create a pattern or 'streak'
rubrics_metrics.description: Three is the minimum number required to create a discernible pattern — two points don’t establish a streak but three do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use at least three items when you want readers to perceive a pattern and expect a continuation; the third occurrence signals a streak and makes the pattern cognitively satisfying. The post cites research that the third repeat is pivotal to believing a streak is occurring. Anti-pattern: using only one or two items where a pattern is intended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-option anchoring (middle choice as default)
rubrics_metrics.description: A series of three offers a concrete 'middle' choice that readers perceive as the best or most popular option.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use three options in pricing or service tiers to steer readers toward the middle (anchoring). This is a practical SaaS/service-provider tactic: present basic, premium, and mid-tier to make the middle look like the best value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the natural cadence of triplets
rubrics_metrics.description: Three has a naturally satisfying cadence — when read aloud the voice typically moves on the second item, creating rhythm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write triples to exploit spoken/listening rhythm: arrange words so the cadence emphasizes the punch. Consider how an announcer or narrator would lift or lower on the second item to set up the third for impact. This is useful for copy read aloud (ads, voiceovers) and for scannable web copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place the funny or surprising element last (punchline on item three)
rubrics_metrics.description: When writing a series of three, save the funny word or phrase for the last item in the series to maximize punch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the third item the reversal, shock, or unexpected twist. The final position has the most pay-off because the first two set the pattern and the third breaks or heightens it. Example: list two normal items then an absurd third. Anti-pattern: putting the joke too early so it loses impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use reversal (subvert expectations) as a comedic mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy often comes from surprising or shocking the reader — doing the opposite of what they expect (a reversal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct the first two items to set an obvious expectation, then make the third item contradict or escalate that expectation. Example quote: Jon Stewart’s Thanksgiving line that switches from normal to deadly for shock value. Reversal pairs well with placing the punchline last.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heightening: escalate (or diminish) across the series
rubrics_metrics.description: Heightening means hitting a comedic idea several times in a way that obviously gets more absurd as you go; you can also move in the opposite (diminishing) direction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Progress items in a clear direction (bigger/more bombastic or smaller/more insignificant) so the relationship between items produces humor. Examples: 'safety pin → knife → harpoon cannon' or 'President → 2-term Congressperson → night janitor.' Note: the relationship between items, not any single item, creates the joke. Consider 'hit' frequency and escalation carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply Rule of 3 in specific copy spots
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain places in copy are especially effective for triples: series of examples, comparisons, exaggerations, and intros/lead-ins.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Templates/examples to use: Series of examples — Item 1, Item 2, Unexpected/Absurd Item 3; Comparisons — short simile or analogy with three elements; Exaggerations — three escalating descriptors; Intros/lead-ins — use triples to set tone before the punch. Use these placements to lighten the mood or increase memorability.

rubrics_metrics.name: If extending past three, avoid overstaying the joke
rubrics_metrics.description: You don’t have to stop at three, but if you add more items make sure the joke doesn’t outstay its welcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When adding additional beats beyond the triple (as in some sketches), keep each new item fresh and escalating; trim when the pattern becomes stale. Anti-pattern: continuing a series until the audience tires or the reversal loses impact.
